Each entry below is one **reading**, of a function or of a whole file. An
agent was given its name, signature, neighboring names and comments — never
its body — and wrote down what it expected to find. Then it opened the file.
The gap between the two is the finding. A file's own entry is titled `the file
itself` and asks whether the header at the top describes what is actually in
there.

`read at` is a hash of the body as it was when the reading was made. When it
stops matching the code, the reading is marked STALE and goes back in the
queue.

What this is and how to add to it: [README.md](README.md)

It also implements a durable "materialization authority" protocol (lock files, tokens, markers, atomic no-clobber rename/publish) so multi-stage writes can be crash-recovered and resumed safely across process restarts, with platform-specific backends (Linux openat2, macOS renameatx_np) and a large embedded suite of property/race tests validating the locking and recovery invariants.

It also implements a durable two-phase-commit \"materialization authority\" protocol (writing->ready temp-file rename, bootstrap authority files, OS+process-local advisory locks, tokens) for crash-safe first-time publication of not-yet-existing logical roots, with Linux openat2/renameat2 and macOS dlsym-resolved renameatx_np backends, plus an ~80-test embedded suite covering races, cross-process locking, and recovery scenarios.

- expected: A test that simulates a waiter blocked on a publication lock file whose backing inode becomes orphaned/non-authoritative (e.g. the lock file is removed or replaced out from under it, perhaps by another process crashing without releasing cleanly). It asserts the waiter detects that the inode it's watching is no longer authoritative and wakes up/proceeds rather than blocking forever, verifying the lock-wait logic doesn't deadlock on stale lock state.
- found: A thread blocks acquiring an OS exclusive flock() on the publication lock file (opened before release). The main thread releases publication authority (which removes/replaces the lock file), so the waiter's flock succeeds on the now-unlinked/orphaned inode. The test verifies that the current directory entry's identity no longer matches the waiter's inode (entry_identity mismatch), then shows a fresh open+lock on the current inode can still succeed concurrently, proving flock-on-a-removed-inode is not authoritative and callers must re-check entry identity rather than trusting a successful lock.
- predicted: some · documented: none · derivable: yes · legible: some · trap: yes
- note: This isn't about a wake/notify mechanism at all — it exercises the well-known flock-on-unlinked-inode hazard: acquiring a lock on a filename doesn't guarantee it's still the file that name points to, so lock code must re-verify entry identity after locking, otherwise two writers can both believe they hold 'the' publication lock.

## src/convert/pipeline/tool.rs

### the file itself
- spec 3 · read at `96f3d858c6b4` · commit `a6d7e33` · read by claude-sonnet-5 · via claude · when 2026-08-21T02:38:35Z · by ross@rossturk.com · cold reading · reading 1 of its run · priming: CLAUDE.md excluded

## src/tui/preemphasis/mod.rs

### the file itself
- spec 3 · read at `4422384e788b` · commit `1681528` · read by claude-sonnet-5 · via claude · when 2026-08-20T07:08:56Z · by ross@rossturk.com · cold reading · reading 5 of its run · priming: CLAUDE.md excluded
